doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: The 'lightning arranger' and first arrangement of 'Sweet Georgia Brown'
summary: A one-dollar mail-order transposing wheel from Billboard led the high school senior to write his first five-part arrangement, astonishing his bandmates.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I want to go back to this music chord transposer, this device.

Oh it was called a “lightning arranger.” Yeah. That was about 1934, I was a junior in high school, or no, I was a senior by then. And I was playing with this little band. We were playing stocks you know. And we had trumpet, trombone — well we never could get a good second trumpet. We usually had trumpet and trombone and sometimes if we had a bigger gig we’d have three brass. And three saxes and drums and piano. And we could never get a good bass player. And we’d play stocks. But anyway we played for the school dances you know. And one day I was looking for something in my dad’s room. And he was secretary of the musicians’ union in Attleboro, Massachusetts, played trombone in the marching band you know, and took care of their business for them. And I was looking for something in the desk and he subscribed to Billboard magazine. And I started thumbing through it. And down in the lower right corner, I remember it was the right hand page, was a little box about, I don’t know, a couple inches, less than a couple of inches high, it said “Lightning Arranger.” I can’t remember the wording, but learn to arrange overnight, you know, instantaneous arranging. What it was, it was a transposing device. And in this way — is it okay if I write, oh I don’t have a pencil, yeah I think I have something. It was — we used to call it celluloid. Is it okay if I write on here? Now we call it plastic. But it was about, let me see I’ll get this up to the camera after, okay, and I’ll give you an idea. Because it’s easy to understand if you see this. There was, okay, I won’t go this whole, but I’ll show you how one of the wheels would look. Okay. Now there were two plastic pieces, and you know picture one of these and then another one. And in between there was a wheel in here, see? And you could turn the wheels here. Then there were slots. I didn’t put all the slots in. And you could turn it over and there were more slots see, on the back. So here would say like it would say concert instruments, like piano. It would give a C chord. You’d have a C, a G, E and a C. The C chord. Then here it would say B flat trumpets. And it would say D, A, F sharp, D. Then here would say E flat saxophones, which would be what A, E, C sharp A you know. And so you had the C chord here, and if you wanted to write for with what I play trumpet, we had a trumpet, E flats, and we had tenor saxophone, which also comes under the heading of the trumpets, you know, the B flat trumpet. So I could write a C chord for those four instruments, and know what notes to write for them. And then over on this side here, on these slots over here, this would say C7.
Okay, we’ve got the dominant chords coming.

And this would be for C7, and then there would be slots that say ninths. Here would say diminished, augmented, and you’d turn over and you’d have the whole ball of wax. So I thought this was great. So I took the ninth thing and I put it down and I just happened to have it on F7 see? So I played the F7, no I had it on F9, no I had an F7. So I played the F7, and I turned the wheel, and I just accidentally turned it in the direction of the cycle of

the fifths. And the next slot was B flat 7. So I struck the B flat 7 and held the thing down. I turned it another notch and hit the E flat 7. Wow. That’s “Sweet Georgia Brown,” you know? And so I wrote my first arrangement, and I turned it over and I did, instead of F7 I did the ninth chords. And I did “Sweet Georgia Brown,” for trumpet, trombone and three saxes. And I used the five way, no double lead you know. And it was like Duke was writing in those days. And I brought that into the guys and they fell on the floor [scats]. And you know with just five ways — imagine what that sound — nobody had ever heard anything like that. You know they weren’t writing like that then.
